AI Mode, AI Overviews, and traditional Search are becoming one product. What Google’s Q3 earnings call revealed about the agentic era.

Even though Wall Street is panicking over Google’s earnings call, it seems obvious to me what is happening. They are not going to slow down when it comes to AI. Throughout the call, they spoke of agents and how we are in the early days of how they are changing Search. They told us that AI Mode, AI overviews, and traditional Search are becoming one unified product.

They also said to expect rapid improvement because of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Things are about to get very interesting.

I think new opportunities are arising, but also much of the way we have traditionally been able to make money from Search is disappearing.

If you prefer video, I share my thoughts on the call.

The main thing I took away from this earnings call is the emphasis on the shift to agentic search. I think this is still unfolding and no one fully knows what this new era of the web will look like. Google gave us a few hints in this call.

I find it fascinating how Google’s stock plummeted after this call. Alphabet’s revenues were up 25% YOY and Cloud revenue was up 103%. The general concern seems to be that Google is pushing AI Mode more, and so far there are fewer opportunities for ads shown in AI Mode. Therefore, revenue from Search is lower than expected. Still, Search advertising is up 12% YOY. (Wall Street was expecting 15%.)

I have no concerns over Google’s ability to continue to thrive. They mentioned in the call that their first priority is to make AI Mode a quality product and then it will focus more on monetizing it. Last week, Google announced that ads in AI Mode were expanding to more countries including Australia, Canada and more.

“Our approach is deliberate – prioritizing the user experience and engagement first, then scaling the formats.”

Mark my word, Google will make plenty of money from ads in the years to come. I think the new connected apps (see more on this below) could eventually be offered as ads.

They also spoke extensively about how there is incredible demand for Google’s computing power. It talked about TPUs not as chip sales, but as systems. “TPU Systems” were mentioned 35 times in the call. Thomas Kurian said:

“A TPU System is not just a chip, but it’s a specialized system that combines multiple things, including hardware, computer, storage, networking and so we are selling much more than just a chip. Software, training, inference.”

I mention this because Google will likely see incredible growth as more and more customers purchase these TPU systems.

What’s most interesting to me is how Google’s verbiage has shifted when it comes to talking about AI Mode and its relationship to Search.

The idea of traditional Search and AI Search merging into one product was mentioned several times:

“We are building one seamless experience across AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Traditional Search.”

“We think of Search holistically, a unified product spanning traditional results and AI powered Search.

I know it feels like Google is behind when it comes to having an agentic product. X has Grokbot. OpenAI has Dots, and Meta’s Muse is taking off. It seems clear to me that the vision of AI being our personal assistant has been in Google’s mind for some time. I think they’re taking their time to fully unpack it all because they need to get it right. Google’s end game here is not just an agent that will help us get things done online, but much bigger!

In May of 2025, Demis Hassabis wrote about Google’s dream of building what they called a “Universal AI Assistant.” Much of this piece discussed Google’s Genie world models acting as training environments for robots and how Project Astra which is now in Gemini Live, will allow us to have insight on the world around us. Google’s mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.

I see the pieces coming together. It starts with online agents and will eventually expand into every aspect of our lives especially as the technology develops for intelligent eyewear and in-home robots.

“We are in the early stages of agentic experiences across our surfaces, and excited about the commercial opportunities ahead.”

He went on to speak about how they started by building agentic experiences into Gemini Enterprise first and, “as a next step [they’re] bringing these features to Search.”

“It’s clear that the agentic capabilities we all envision are going to be real.”

“I’m excited about agents, and I would view it as a new frontier, which brings in a new set of use cases to Search.”

Those new use cases likely start with Connected Apps.

By the way, if you want to be ahead of the curve in seeing how businesses are adapting to agentic search, I send out an email every week with all of the latest news on Search & AI:

On the day of the call, Google announced the Connected Apps Platform. There are already a handful of apps that can be used via MCP by Gemini either in the app or from within Search. Here is an example they gave where a user calls @Peloton to bring the Peloton app experience into their agentic flow within Gemini.

You can apply to the Connected Apps Platform here.

It was six months ago that Sundar Pichai said in an interview that “Search will be an agent manager.” I think this will be a new era where we shift from Search being a place to find websites that have information to a place where you use tools to help you (or your agents) get things done.

“The Gemini app is now at one billion users and is the fastest growing product in Google’s History.”

A billion users is the same number reported by ChatGPT in June of 2026.

I find this fascinating because my own use of the Gemini app has declined significantly. I use Gemini in Antigravity for almost everything.

We all know that Google’s models have not been as advanced as those from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Last week, Google announced a new frontier model, just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. Gemini 4 Carbon is currently undergoing voluntary testing as per the U.S. Government’s recommendations and will soon be released. Artificial Analysis currently has Carbon listed as the most intelligent model to date.

On the call, Sundar Pichai said that more models are coming soon, including “more efficient versions to help developers optimize for speed and cost.”

He said they started seeing a step change with Gemini 3.8 Flash when it came to coding internally at Google. And then Gemini 4 Argon was a “huge point of inflection.” He said:

“It is one of the most meaningful internal productivity levers [they] have seen on software engineering, directly tracking high-quality code that’s getting checked in, and the rate at which it’s getting checked in.”

“Carbon is a meaningful step up from Argon.”

Right now I use Gemini 4 Argon across three or four simultaneous Antigravity conversations most of the day long. On the Ultra plan, I have barely touched my quota. I thought 3.8 Flash was amazing. It helped me start to automate many of the SEO reports I run. When I switched to Gemini 4 Argon a mind blowing thing happened. Gemini 4 Argon + my internal OKF powered knowledge brain and my algo update MCP started producing far better consulting reports than I could alone. I truly believe we are not far from the day where AI will be better at all knowledge work than even the best humans in their field.

Last week, Google announced Genie 4, its latest world model. While it’s cool to see how it can generate interesting scenes and games, the most exciting thing about this model is that it will be used to create training simulations for AI agents and also for robots.

“Beyond our Gemini 4 series, yesterday we announced Genie 4, our most advanced world model yet that simulates safe, realistic, interactive worlds with native audio in real time. This is an important building block for training robots and agents.”

“I would expect the next twelve months to see continued acceleration because of RSI.”

Buckle up. RSI is “Recursive Self Improvement.” AI is being used more and more to help improve AI. We will see it improve rapidly.

Here’s the call if you’d like to listen to it.

#7350. Product Manager - Auth at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We're hiring a Product Manager for Supabase Auth. You'll own the surface area that developers use to authenticate and authorize their end users and manage identity in their apps: email, phone and social login, passkeys and MFA, enterprise SSO, the OAuth 2.1 server, auth hooks, and support for organizations and multi-tenant applications.

You'll work closely with the Auth engineering team and with partners across Product Management, Security, Design and GTM.

This role is ideal for someone who’s excited about building tools for millions of developers and who has a strong understanding of existing and emerging authentication practices and protocols.

You'll collaborate with customers of all sizes and expertise levels. Indie developers shipping a side project, startups choosing their first auth stack, SaaS teams designing multi-tenant access, and enterprises in security review.

You'll own the problem statements and solution rationale behind the Auth roadmap. This means working with Engineering and Design to shape how Supabase crafts the developer experience for the problems you’ve prioritized solving.

You'll define how Auth works for AI agents on Supabase: agents that sign users up, act on their behalf, and call APIs.

You'll use data to understand how Supabase developers are using Auth features: where they succeed, where they get stuck, and what to tackle first.

You'll keep Engineering, Design and GTM aligned. You'll own the plan of record for what's coming, why, and in what order.

5+ years of Product Management experience on developer tools, or are an ex-founder with equivalent depth. You're comfortable commenting on an architecture doc, following a design discussion, and advocating for the user when trade-offs are required.

Have shipped standards-based auth or identity products. You've owned OAuth/OIDC, SAML, SCIM, sessions or token design, and you know from experience where each one breaks for customers.

Work comfortably with corporate buyers and with developers. You can work through a CISO's security review and an indie developer's bug report in the same week. You have intuition on which enterprise asks are real value-adding requirements and which are checkbox items.

Are comfortable with Postgres and familiar with row-level security.

Work async by default. Supabase is fully remote. You make decisions in writing and move work forward without meetings.

Owned auth or identity inside an integrated cloud platform.

Ran an organizations, tenancy, or SSO+SCIM launch from start to finish.

Designed auth for agents or other automated systems: OAuth for MCP clients, machine-to-machine credentials, scoped tokens.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7349. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7345. Google’s Search Volume Is About 5x ChatGPT’s, OpenAI Says via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

ChatGPT's search-like queries equal about a fifth of Google's volume, its maker says, counting each question that sends it to the web. Traffic data differs.

ChatGPT receives roughly one-fifth as many search-like queries as does Google, according to ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry.

The point he made about the volume of search-like queries was shared with Alex Kantrowitz in an open discussion during a Monday evening dinner in New York hosted by OpenAI. The transcript was later posted by Big Technology on Tuesday.

OpenAI counts a search each time a question sends ChatGPT to the web, Fry said. The visits ChatGPT sends to websites are a separate measure, and outside data on that traffic puts ChatGPT far behind Google.

Alex Kantrowitz of Big Technology asked Fry whether a conversation that includes a search counts as one, or whether each question requiring a web search counts separately. Fry replied:

“Every time you ask a question and go search the web, that’s a search.”

He said people first came to ChatGPT mostly for writing and coding help, which they wouldn’t have searched for. Over the past year, he said, they’ve brought questions about people, places and things that need up-to-date information, plus finance and health questions, where ChatGPT does a web search. He described the category as anything users would have taken to a traditional search engine.

Fry, in the published interview, did not reveal which Google figure was referenced; for how long the comparison is based on; nor does he state which regions are covered. He has also been asked if one-fifth of Google’s size makes ChatGPT multiple times bigger than Bing. The report by Big Technology indicates that the number of weekly active users of ChatGPT grew by 20% (from 1 billion to 1.2 billion) over the last two months.

In February, Ahrefs had estimated the search volume of ChatGPT to be around 12 percent that of Google’s search volume using a definition of search that was different from that used by OpenAI. It began with 2.5 billion daily ChatGPT prompts in July 2025 (from a study by Harvard University and OpenAI) and determined that approximately 65 percent were the type of query users would have previously looked up on Google.

Using this data, it compared those numbers with the over 5 trillion searches per year Google announced in March 2025. The author said that 65% was higher than the share the researchers had classified as search. That method sorts prompts by the kind of request, while Fry’s figure counts web searches.

Ahrefs also tracks where traffic to websites comes from across sites that use its free Web Analytics tool. In October, across 118,671 sites, Google accounted for 24.74% of tracked traffic and ChatGPT for 0.36%, according to the tracker’s Nov. 3 update.

Alphabet’s third-quarter release, which I covered on Oct. 28, gives Google’s search query growth as a rate rather than a count. In the release, CEO Sundar Pichai said AI investments are driving overall search query growth and that Google’s “year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”

OpenAI’s data comparing search-like queries by users of ChatGPT versus those using Google indicates the approximate 1/5th ratio. Fry’s counting rule includes only the search requests made by ChatGPT users in order to send a question to the Web. Ahrefs’ referral tracker tracks the number of visitors that are directed to websites. In this data set, Google has an overwhelming amount of referrals compared to ChatGPT.

Neither Fry’s number nor Google’s year-over-year growth rate illustrates if ChatGPT searches are replacing searches on Google. If ChatGPT’s size is included in a channel plan, then when reporting search it should be accompanied by the definitions of query volume and referral traffic, which will provide two different metrics.

Ahrefs’ tracker reports referral shares month by month, giving you a regular outside perspective on the traffic ChatGPT sends. OpenAI’s roughly one-fifth ratio is difficult to compare with other estimates until the company clarifies which Google figure it used.

#7340. Reddit Is Going Logged-In Only – Brands Still Need To Be In The Conversation via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Reddit conversations still shape purchase decisions through search and AI, giving brands reasons to stay engaged and watch how login tests affect access.

Reddit’s Q3 Earnings Call got a lot of attention in the last few days, specifically for an announcement to start moving towards a more logged-in experience. I understand the attention and worry some marketers have expressed, but having listened to the entire conversation, as well as the ModWorld AMA interview, I do not find myself concerned about the future of Reddit or its influence in search and LLMs.

I will get into that more in a second, but another really big point worth highlighting is how important Reddit has become to the user’s journey online.

Reddit reported an average of 515.2 million weekly active uniques in Q3. That isn’t a count of people shopping, but it gives some context for the size of the platform where these decisions are being discussed.

In my experience, Google often helps people narrow their options, and Reddit helps them validate the decision. Once someone has figured out which products might solve their problem, they want to know what happened when another person actually used them, what went wrong, and whether the recommendation still makes sense for their situation.

In Reddit’s May 2026 survey, half of the U.S. respondents said they verify AI recommendations on Reddit.*

In its Q3 shareholder letter and earnings call, Reddit said it plans to begin testing a logged-in experience in select markets outside the U.S. during Q4. Steve Huffman was clear that Reddit is going to make this change, but the tests will help figure out where and when someone needs to log in.

He also said Reddit wants shared links to keep working and described leaving some access available for people coming from search, opening a shared post, or trying Reddit for the first time. My reading is that someone could still get to the conversation they came for, with the login requirement appearing as they try to go further into Reddit. Reddit still needs to figure out where that login prompt belongs.

That’s a familiar approach for a social platform, and Huffman pointed to peers that have already made this transition. Reddit wants more people using a personalized experience, better signals for advertising, and more control over access to its data. I can see why Reddit would want those things, even if someone dropping in to read a conversation would rather skip the account.

I would still watch what happens in the tests because asking people to log in can affect whether they stay, come back, or join the conversation. Keeping a linked post accessible also doesn’t guarantee that Google’s rankings stay the same or that every LLM can continue accessing Reddit in the same way. But I didn’t hear a reason to jump straight to the conclusion that Reddit is shutting off discovery through search and AI.

Huffman also said data licensing discussions are continuing, including access for training and use within products. There wasn’t a new deal announced, and he left open the possibility of declining a deal. Those conversations are worth following alongside the login tests, without assuming that one tells us how the other will turn out.

See also: Reddit Wants To Be The Destination, Not Just The Source Behind Search & AI

Reddit was already receiving less search traffic before these login tests. Huffman said the decline accelerated during Q3 and continued into October. He pointed to Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode as major factors, with lower rankings for machine-translated content as another possible explanation.

Pew’s study of U.S. browsing in March 2025 found that people clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, compared with 15% without one. A link within the summary received a click on 1% of visits with a summary. That isn’t a measurement of Reddit’s current traffic, but it gives us some context for the click-through concerns.

Fewer clicks don’t mean those Reddit threads aren’t being used. I see Reddit conversations referenced in AI Overviews all the time, helping shape the answers people get. Someone can learn from that conversation and use it to make a decision without opening the thread.

People can still click through from an AI Overview, and those visits still matter. From a search marketing standpoint, I also see value in Reddit threads showing up in the results, being referenced in an answer, and helping shape what people learn about a brand or product.

See also: Reddit Preserved The Part Of The Internet We Broke

These are the conversations where people get into whether a product will work for their situation, what went wrong when someone else used it, and which trade-offs they’re willing to accept. Someone explains their circumstances, another person challenges a recommendation, and the replies bring out a detail that changes the decision.

If people keep asking the same question about your product, there’s something they haven’t been able to figure out. If they keep recommending a competitor for a particular situation, there’s a reason worth understanding. Being present gives you an opportunity to learn from those conversations and help where your experience is relevant, while respecting how that community works.

Those same conversations can help shape what someone learns about your brand when they find them through search or see them referenced in an AI answer. I would want to understand what people are saying, where they’re getting stuck, and what someone from the company could explain that would help them make a decision.

It always makes me think back to something my co-founder at OGS Media, Bartosz Goralewicz, once said: “Reddit is the only website I know of that told search engines, ‘Pay us, or we’ll pull our content.'”

Reddit’s a continuously evolving platform, and its place online keeps adjusting and shifting, but those conversations continue to be valuable, both to the people making decisions and to the search and AI platforms using them.

*Survey source: Reddit/Attest, May 2026. The survey covered U.S. adults ages 18-65 who use social media, LLMs, and ecommerce monthly, with a full U.S. sample of 13,956 respondents.

#7336. Threads adds more community champion badges

The digital display cards are designed to highlight users who have become key contributors in their topical subgroups.

Threads has added new community champion badges to recognize top contributors in topical communities, while it's also doubling the number of recognized champions in communities.

As shown in this example, posted by NBA Threads champion Brian Moller, key contributors in Threads communities will be rewarded with these new digital, flippable badges, which they'll then be able to share with others in the app to highlight their community engagement.

As explained by Threads: “Champions make their communities feel like home, and earn their badges by bringing people together and keeping the conversation going.”

Threads said that community champions will be able to manage flair and custom reactions for their communities. Threads added custom flair tags to communities in July.

In a separate post, Threads Chief Connor Hayes said that communities have become "a central part" of Threads as more people come to the app to participate in topical discussion.

Hayes added that Threads wants to build on community engagement by adding more topic groups including NWSL, PWHL and NFL fanbases, as well as location-based groups, such as ohiothreads and memphis.

Launched in September 2025, Threads communities provide an easier way for users to find their people by bringing together like-minded people in searchable, topic-based discussions.

In June, as part of Meta’s announcement that Threads had reached 500 million users, the company said that communities was one of the fastest-growing features in the app.

#7334. The 11 SEO Features Every CMS Should Ship With (Most Still Don’t) via @sejournal, @sallymills

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Cut recurring developer tickets with CMS SEO essentials like canonical tags and indexing controls, plus automation, redirect safeguards, and real examples.

Content management systems (CMS) often try to force SEOs into a box of “this is how a website should work.” The problem is that SEO has never been a black-and-white thing and so often depends upon the individual website, industry, and brand as to how we may want to structure indexing, content, and infrastructure.

Over my years as an in-house SEO, consultant, and web developer, I’ve worked with a wide range of CMS. Even though we continue to see improvements across platforms, many still fail to meet the base-level requirements and flexibility we as SEOs need day-to-day. This results in us as an industry being on repeat, submitting the same ticket for a fix again and again.

What do I consider to be the actual bare minimum a CMS should offer for SEOs and content creators? Every week I continue to find out about often well-known platforms missing what I would consider a baseline standard.

On three different systems this year, I’ve watched teams need a developer to implement canonical tags – Google, Microsoft, and Yahoo announced the tag together back in 2009! You’d think we’d have this sorted by now.

On Webflow, I’ve had to hardcode HTML tables into the page because the editor doesn’t have built-in HTML table support. I’ve found having semantically correct HTML incredibly important to help bots understand the content.

And on WordPress, you have no way to edit your robots.txt out-of-the-box, exclude pages from the sitemap, or noindex individual pages without the help of a developer or accessing your source files. This often forces users to install bloated SEO plugins to manage what I would consider the basics of SEO.

In my opinion, every CMS that considers SEO, and wants to be crawlable and accessible by bots, should have the following:

If your content is a list, show it in an unordered or ordered list.

If your content is in the sidebar, put it in an aside HTML element.

I’ve recently seen this issue with Shopify preventing you from removing pages from sitemaps when you are using an additional market as sitemaps “are generated automatically and include all market-specific URLs.”

I’ve worked across numerous platforms over my time with many having a constant stream of content, development, and marketing changes going live. Often teams find themselves raising the same ticket again and again. Over the years, there have been a few CMS improvements that development teams and I have implemented to help improve speed to market.

See also: Ask An SEO: How Do You Prioritize Technical SEO Fixes With Limited Dev Support?

Having a table of contents at the start of your content is hugely beneficial to the user and can earn you sitelinks in Google’s search results. Often, systems can make this quite a manual job to create, forcing the content creator to manually create each link and ID tag for the headings of the page.

A good CMS should automate this task completely by grabbing the H2s of the page and pulling them into the component. To go above and beyond, they should also allow you to exclude specific headings and choose whether to include H3s and H4s.

I’ve had to get this built by a developer in enterprise CMSs. Even WordPress needs a plugin like Rank Math to do it, which tells you how far down the list it sits for most platforms.

SEOs can often become maintenance people, cleaning up broken links, redirecting pages that are gone, then, of course, cleaning up internal links that are now redirecting. There are a few different levels of automation that CMSs could offer to reduce the manual workload of SEOs.

I’ve worked on large editorial websites where there simply isn’t the resource to go through and replace each link that redirects.

The biggest run I’ve done was after a migration of a site with tens of thousands of URLs from an old .NET platform to a new CMS. Every internal link on the site still pointed at the old URL and hopped through a redirect to get to the new one. We wrote a Python script against the CMS API that followed each link to its final destination and rewrote it, so nobody had to fix links by hand.

Having this script run regularly ensures bots spend less time on old URLs, users get to their destinations quicker, and the business spends less time on manual cleanup tasks.

A CMS should also be flagging when a page’s URL has been changed and automatically adding a 301 redirect from the old URL to the new. This change would reduce delayed clean-up from SEOs and would result in a better user experience.

If they wanted to go above and beyond, a clean-up script should be scheduled to automatically update any internal links that still point to the old URL. Extra points if the system could suggest a relevant URL to redirect to.

We often have to rely on technical SEO tools to report on 404 errors. I think in today’s world of monitoring, CMSs should offer offer a report of broken links and allow SEOs to bulk upload the correct links or decide to remove the link. So often, we find ourselves having to edit 404 links one by one – and often the same link.

It’s still incredibly rare that we have systems that offer the functionality to set a URL or a folder of URLs to a 410 status code. To this day, I’ve only used a 410 a few times on a live site. With most CMSs not providing this functionality, SEOs tend to land on redirecting or leaving as a 404.

Most platforms these days have some form of redirect manager; however, so often they are missing important customization and safeguards.

Guardrails matter more than any other item on this list. I once took an entire website down with a single stray pipe character in a regex redirect rule. One | in the wrong place matched every URL on the site and sent all of them to the same page. A redirect manager that tested the rule against a sample of URLs before saving would have caught it in seconds.

To this day, I haven’t found a CMS that does a great job of handling different image files. Often they’ll have a range of issues that negatively impact SEO.

One of my biggest gripes is the messy and multiple different versions of an image URL. One enterprise system I’ve worked with would add an ID to every image file, and applying different optimizations like sizing or cropping within the platform would result in numerous different URLs. And you could still reference the image directly without the ID. For websites where image search is vital, this could cause major duplication issues.

Previously, it was an absolute requirement for me to have a CMS that allowed for either bulk importing content changes through CSV or API alongside a Python script. With the way AI is changing our work processes, having the ability to connect your AI agent through CLI or MCP is incredibly helpful.

As of this year, I’m finding myself making fewer changes directly in a CMS and instead connecting to MCPs or CLI. If you are running your own WordPress environment, I would recommend testing out the Claude Code and CLI connection. On some of my websites, I can now update content and development work directly from Claude.

As always with anything AI and connecting to public websites, make sure you have testing processes and guardrails set up to ensure that you don’t break anything important.

In big businesses, we often see repeatable small tickets take up developers’ time that simply require them to upload a new marketing script to the HTML head or the top of the body. One of the best time-saving opportunities is to provide a CMS settings section that allows you to add scripts manually.

In the past, this has given me the flexibility to quickly trial new schemas, tracking tools, and metadata.

However, this does require trust between the development and marketing teams, as it is a way to break something. So always include code validation and a release process to protect your website.

Every CMS is going to be different, so the best thing you can do is work with what you have. People often ask me for a CMS recommendation, and in very SEO style I say, “It depends.” And often, we aren’t the person who gets to make that decision.

I encourage everyone to problem-solve and try to automate where possible. Analyze where you or the team are spending most of your time and which tickets keep coming up time and time again. Work closely with developers to build out solutions that can grow as the business grows and give you the flexibility to implement yourself.

#7328. Reach Is Losing As A Paid Media KPI: 4 Signals From Jupiter Festival Miami For 2027 via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Build your 2027 paid media plan around attention, creator content, and streaming inventory, with tests that tie new metrics to incremental sales.

If you manage paid search, paid social, or programmatic budgets, the first Jupiter Festival Miami just handed you a 2027 planning problem. The executives who buy and sell premium video spent three days saying that reach is no longer the number that matters. And the money is already moving toward creators, attention-weighted media, and new streaming inventory to back that up.

That matters to PPC people more than it might seem. When the people setting brand budgets change the KPI, the performance team eventually inherits the new scorecard.

I’ve been looking for signals like this at industry conferences since I entered the field in 2002. The speakers at the good ones share strategic insights, critical data, and tactical advice that fly under the radar, because organizers know conventional wisdom won’t fill seats or bring attendees back next year. So, they book people who work at the leading edge of the leading edge.

Jupiter Festival ran from Oct. 6 to 9, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. Its organizers say more than 2,300 media, entertainment, and sports leaders attended. Art Basel’s parent, MCH Group, took a 20% stake in June. The IAB signed up as a founding partner, and YouTube was the founding sponsor.

I didn’t attend. But I reviewed the daily recaps the festival’s publicists sent me, then checked what the speakers said against published data. Four signals held up.

Jasmine Dawson, senior VP of digital at BBC Studios, on a Day 1 panel about building fandoms that brands can activate said, “Reach should not be the primary KPI.” A big reach number is great for the media owner, she added, but it says nothing about whether the audience will do anything next.

Her distinction was that “building an audience is not fandom and fandom is not audience.”

On Day 2, Marc Guldimann, CEO and co-founder of Adelaide, put a measurement frame around the same idea. “If you want to rate the quality of an opportunity, look at the probability of attention,” he said during a panel with YouTube’s U.S. managing director Brian Albert and Evan Shapiro of ESHAP. Brands, he added, are now telling the whole ecosystem that they care more about quality.

That isn’t a throwaway line from Guldimann. Adelaide’s AU metric scores media placements from 0 to 100 on their likelihood of capturing attention and driving outcomes. Its 2026 Outcomes Guide covers 60 campaigns. And on Oct. 14, a week after Miami, the company launched a partner designation program for survey and outcome partners whose data can be matched directly to AU.

Shapiro pushed the argument furthest. Three days before he unveiled the 2026 Creator Ecosphere Map on stage on Oct. 8, he previewed it in a Substack post headlined “The Era of Reach is Over. Welcome to The Affinity Era.” The map ranks creators by follower count and, alongside that, grades each one on an affinity score.

Three speakers from three corners of the business, the seller, the measurement vendor, and the analyst, landed in the same place. That’s what an emerging trend looks like before it shows up in a platform’s reporting interface.

Here’s my take. Paid search people will be tempted to shrug, because search has never been a reach business. But your YouTube, CTV, and Demand Gen line items probably still report on impressions, CPM, and view rate. Those are reach metrics. If the brand side starts asking for quality-weighted numbers in 2027, the performance team that already has them will own that conversation.

See also: How Do I Measure And Attribute When Clicks Only Tell Part Of The Story? – Ask A PPC

The Day 3 panel “Direct to Fan: How Creators Are Building the New Media Stack” included Amanda Tarpey, head of creator and creative at YouTube Ads. Her read on advertisers was that marketers are “waking up” to the trust, influence, and authenticity creators have. “They’re saying: I can’t afford to miss that,” she said. “There’s a lot of experimentation, but the infrastructure is not standardized.”

That second sentence is the one PPC teams should underline.

The IAB’s own numbers show why. Its 2025 Creator Economy Ad Spend & Strategy Report found that 48% of creator ad buyers now consider creators a “must buy,” ranking them just behind paid search and social media. The report put U.S. creator ad spend at $37.1 billion in 2025 and projected $43.9 billion for 2026, according to Digiday’s breakdown of the report.

The split is where paid media comes in. Digiday reports that $13.2 billion of the 2026 total is expected to go to paid amplification of creator content on social media, up 48% from $8.9 billion. Another $11.1 billion goes to amplifying that content beyond social, up 56% from $7.1 billion. In other words, a growing share of “creator marketing” is really ad buying with creator-made creative.

The creators on stage explained the pull. Joakim Noah, the former NBA player who hosts the YouTube series NOMAD, said what he loves about YouTube is controlling his content and “connecting with an audience that is completely different from what you’re used to.” Hudson Matter, a YouTuber and CEO of NextWave Media, called YouTube “one of the most powerful platforms in the world.”

One correction is needed, though. Matter also said, “almost half of the world is on YouTube.” Alphabet doesn’t publish a monthly user count, but DataReportal puts YouTube’s ad reach at about 2.77 billion people a month, roughly a third of the world’s population. That’s closer to half of internet users than half of the world. Use the smaller number in your deck.

My view is that Tarpey’s “not standardized” warning is the real opportunity here. When the infrastructure is messy, the team that can run creator content through the same testing, bidding, and conversion tracking discipline it applies to search ads becomes the team that gets the budget.

See also: Why Running YouTube Ads Like Search Will Burn Your Budget

Scott Young, co-founder and chief product officer of Transmit, made the most practical point of Day 1. “With streaming, you have the opportunity to aggregate valuable ad supply that would have otherwise gotten lost,” he said. He singled out women’s sports, which he said are growing on free ad-supported streaming.

Transmit is the plumbing behind that claim. Its software creates in-stream ad units, such as picture-in-picture placements during live games, without adding more traditional ad breaks. The company was selected for the Google Ad Manager Technology Partner Program, which connects that “in-moment” inventory to Google Ad Manager’s programmatic pipes for live and on-demand video.

For anyone buying through Google’s stack or a DSP, that’s the part to watch. New premium sports inventory that used to be sold only through direct deals is starting to show up as programmatic supply.

The women’s sports thread ran through all three days. On Day 2, WNBA legend Lisa Leslie talked about welcoming new fans while staying true to loyal ones. Colie Edison, the WNBA’s chief growth officer, said customers are “three times more likely to purchase from a brand that they support.” I couldn’t find the study behind that number, so treat it as a claim, not a benchmark. On Day 3, LA Sparks president Stacy Johns said it’s on the teams “to create the content and interesting moments for brands to show up authentically.”

There’s a budgeting catch for 2027, too. NBCUniversal Telemundo’s Claudia Chagui described turning Rockefeller Center into a FIFA World Cup fan village this summer. Big live events like that, plus a costly U.S. midterm cycle, inflated 2026. EMARKETER projects total U.S. media ad spending growth will slow from 15.6% in 2026 to 9.4% in 2027, and it warns that CTV budgets built around tournament and election inventory should expect to normalize.

Anish Melwani, former chairman and CEO of LVMH North America and co-founder of 22 Montaigne Entertainment, described a decade-long tug of war that every performance marketer will recognize. Luxury marketing evolved toward “more lower funnel performance,” he said, “but great luxury brands understand how much you have to keep doing at the top in order for that to make a difference.”

He also drew a line between formats. Luxury will keep looking for “pockets of premium,” he said, while other brands look at two-minute microdramas, and the two occupy different places in consumers’ minds.

Shapiro predicted the same format shift from the other direction. “Like cable in the ’80s, you will see an explosion of premium vertical content in the next 18 months,” he said, adding that brands not engaging “will get left behind.”

Others argued that the brand itself should become the content. McDonald’s VP of marketing Elizabeth Campbell and Known president Ross Martin discussed Meal Ticket, the Prime Video documentary tied to the 50th McDonald’s All American Games. Chris Long, CEO of Longshot Productions, the company behind The Beekeeper franchise, said. “If you have the money and means, instead of spending it on a marketing campaign, why not put it in a film where it will live forever?”

Andrew Gottlieb of NBCUniversal’s Rock Studios, the branded content unit NBCU launched at Cannes in June, added the line I’d tape to the monitor of anyone running AI-generated ad variations at scale. “AI can do a lot, and it can create a lot of content, but it can’t make people care about that content.”

Put those together, and the takeaway for PPC teams is uncomfortable. Search and shopping campaigns harvest demand. When brands shift money back to the top of the funnel, the question your CMO will ask is how much of your conversion volume that upper-funnel spend created. If you can’t answer it, someone else will.

See also: How To Measure PPC Performance When AI Controls The Auction

IAB CEO David Cohen gave the line that ties the four signals together. Sitting down on Day 3 with Forbes contributor Howard Homonoff, he said, “The one thing that we simply cannot do is the same thing that we’ve done year-over-year.” Marketers love year-over-year comparisons, he acknowledged, “but if there was a time for a clean sheet of paper and taking advantage of the innovation in the market, it’s now.”

According to festival co-founder William Mellis, as recounted to Net Influencer, Cohen also raised the need for a common currency to measure advertising across fragmented distribution.

I agree with Cohen on the clean sheet. I’d add one condition he didn’t state on stage.

Notice who was making the case against reach in Miami. BBC Studios, YouTube, and Transmit were sponsors, and NBCUniversal and Adelaide sell the alternatives. That doesn’t make them wrong. Sellers often see the shift first because they’re the ones being asked to prove value. But it does mean paid media teams should treat “reach is over” as a hypothesis to test before they budget against it.

Attention scores, affinity grades, and fandom indexes are all better questions than “how many people saw it.” None of them is an answer until you’ve tied it to incremental sales in your own accounts. Ground-truth the new metrics the same way we should have ground-truthed CPM a decade ago.

Here’s how I’d turn the Miami signals into planning moves for a paid media or PPC team this quarter.

1. Add a quality column to every upper-funnel line item. For YouTube, CTV, and programmatic video, report an attention or media quality score next to CPM and view rate. Then run at least one test that compares high-scoring and low-scoring placements on conversion lift, so you know whether the score predicts results in your accounts.

2. Budget for creator content as ad creative. Set aside test money to run creator-made assets through paid formats such as Meta partnership ads, TikTok Spark Ads, or YouTube creator partnerships. Judge them with the same holdouts, bidding strategies, and conversion tracking you use for search, since that discipline is exactly what Tarpey said the market lacks.

3. Reset your year-over-year baseline. If your 2026 numbers include World Cup or midterm-season inventory, flag it before finance compares 2027 against it. Cohen’s advice to stop running the same plan year after year applies to the comparison too.

4. Write the measurement memo before your CMO asks for it. One page that explains how upper-funnel spend feeds your search and shopping conversions, and which test will prove it, is how a PPC manager starts sounding like a director.

Jupiter Festival’s organizers have already put Miami 2027 on the calendar. My bet is that by then, the speakers will have stopped arguing about whether reach is the wrong KPI and started arguing about which replacement is right.

PPC teams that have run their own tests by then will have something worth saying. The rest will be taking notes.

#7325. Companies may need to restrict AI use to manage costs

Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI and Meta have all spent enormous amounts of money to build out their artificial intelligence projects, but have yet to see returns.

The pressure is rising for artificial intelligence projects to show some level of return, with industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic both posting massive losses in their earnings results, and xAI reducing access capacity due to non-viable cost-to-revenue calculations.

First, on OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the biggest AI players, which are both looking to launch their respective IPOs sometime soon.

As reported by Reuters, OpenAI is facing another year of heavy financial losses, with the company recently informing its investors that its projected 2026 revenue could be significantly lower than it had previously forecast.

As per Reuters: “OpenAI has told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop ​from what it signaled earlier, a person familiar with the ‌matter told Reuters on Thursday. The company previously indicated to investors at a separate event that its revenue run rate for last month was approaching $70 billion.”

According to AI Funding Tracker, OpenAI has already weathered more than $20 billion in operating losses in the first half of 2026, with revenue of around $12 billion for the same period. The company had hoped to win more investor confidence ahead of a planned IPO with a better Q3 performance.

But a lower-than-expected revenue result could mean that OpenAI is on track to post a major financial loss in 2026.

Anthropic, meanwhile, recently shared that while its revenue is increasing, its costs are also set to skyrocket as the company spends big to keep up with the evolving AI development race.

As reported by CNBC, Anthropic reported a significant Q3 2026 revenue increase, rising almost 1,127% year over year to $17 billion. At the same time, the company also announced plans to spend more than $895 billion on compute and infrastructure over the next few years.

CNBC added that while Anthropic’s revenue is up 47% quarter over quarter, its compute and infrastructure costs increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared to the same period last year.

Meanwhile, xAI owner Elon Musk told Grok Bot users on Nov. 1 that the company had implemented new restrictions on access because “the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.”

Taken alongside these other notes, this is pretty much a summary of the entire AI industry, as companies pour more and more money into AI projects without a clear revenue pathway to justify that investment.

Meta is facing the same challenges. The company has seen strong early adoption of its Muse agents, which are its big hope for driving consumer AI adoption. However, Meta has also committed hundreds of billions of dollars to AI development and support infrastructure, which sets the bar very high for a cash flow-positive result.

Indeed, based on the company’s existing financial commitments to AI projects, it’s got a long, long way to go.

In 2025, Meta generated $200.97 billion, with $4.8 billion of that coming from non-advertising intake, which includes AI subscriptions.

In order to break even on its current AI spending commitments, Meta would need to generate around $100 billion per year from AI subscriptions and partnerships over the next decade.

In other words, Meta needs to build a whole new business offering that generates half as much income as one of the most profitable businesses in the world if it hopes to even come close to turning its AI investment into a profit anytime before 2036.

The operational cost-to-benefit ratio is almost too high to fathom. Moreover, with AI projects continuing to face opposition and negative perception increasing among consumers, many companies may be forced to reconsider their approaches and re-examine the openness of their AI models.

Restricting usage would reduce costs, as Musk said, but it could also slow adoption.

Then again, maybe taking generative AI tools out of the hands of the public, and reducing the amount of AI slop being published to social apps, would lead to a better outcome overall.

Doing that could also make it cost-prohibitive for scammers to generate AI replicas of other people’s content, which is an issue that Instagram Chief Adam Mosseri recently highlighted as a major concern.

Essentially, the cost crunch could soon see AI tools reducing their usage limits, which could lead to less AI use overall.

The question then is whether Meta will end up winning by eating the losses that other companies can’t in order to maximize the take-up of its Muse agents.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

AI Mode now links home service searches to booking and quote pages. Here's how businesses reach those pages and what partners say about lead fees.

Google is allowing home service businesses to accept bookings and quote requests generated by AI Mode via Partner Platforms such as the Marketplaces (Angi & Thumbtack) and Field Service Software providers (Housecall Pro & Jobber). On X Wednesday, Google Search Product VP, Robby Stein made a statement regarding the changes and stated that this product is available now in the U.S.

For a plumber or cleaning company, the way in is its field service software or marketplace account. Jobber says its eligible U.S. customers can take those requests now with no lead fees. Housecall Pro also says there are no lead fees, though its release says its integration is coming soon.

Today, we’re making it even easier to research & book home services with direct links in AI Mode through partners like @angi_home @thumbtack @housecall & @GetJobber (and @ServiceTitan coming soon). It’s available now in the U.S.

In the video posted, a searcher is asking to get a handyman to come by and build a bed and dresser the next day. AI Mode identifies local handyman services with online availability along with other service providers who are able to provide a quote. The listing of each service provider includes their rating along with a brief description of what they do. The first of these listings also lists two available times for an appointment.

In May at Google’s I/O conference, Google announced plans to roll out its agentic booking experience to cover additional types of local experiences & services, including direct links to finish booking with the provider. At that same event Google stated that users will be able to ask Google to call businesses for them (in areas such as home repair, beauty & pet care) and that both features would be rolled out nationwide this summer. On Wednesday, Google announced links to named partner companies providing access to booking Home Services.

Jobber announced this week that eligible customers in the United States can be found and booked using AI Mode. According to Jobber’s Help Page, there are certain requirements for businesses to appear in AI Mode. The business must have an active and paid Jobber subscription, a full address listed in Jobber and a Google Business Profile connected to Jobber (listed at the same location), and the business must have assigned a request or booking form to Google, and Jobber defaults to connecting these forms to Google. Trial subscriptions cannot appear in AI Mode.

Once Google identifies a matching profile, a “Book Online” button appears on the business’s Google Business Profile with a link directly to the business’ Jobber booking form. Most times Google will find a match within a few days as stated in the help page.

Requests and bookings made through AI Mode come into Jobber just like another online booking would. There is no lead fee associated with these bookings and they follow the schedule and availability that the business has established. For assessment bookings, they are automatically confirmed by Jobber unless the business has turned on an approval feature that allows them to accept or decline each one individually before it is confirmed. In announcing the integration, Jobber CEO Sam Pillar explained that he believes his company should assist professionals in showing up when customers use AI to search “while keeping ownership of the customer relationships they’ve worked hard to build.”

Housecall Pro states that all of its users will be able to show up in AI Mode at no additional charge. When a Homeowner makes a request, it will be sent to the selected Professional’s Housecall Pro account inbox. Co-Founder & Chief AI Officer of Housecall Pro, Roland Ligtenberg describes it as “One request, one Pro, no lead fee, no bidding war.”

According to Housecall Pro’s Partner page, every one of Housecall Pro’s Professionals are auto-enrolled in AI Mode without having anything to do on their part. The available time slots will be pulled from the Professional’s Calendar, and according to the partner page, no Google Business Profile is required for a Professional to show up in AI Mode. However, the release does say that the integration is coming soon to eligible US Customers.

Angi says homeowners who select an Angi pro that shows up in AI Mode will go straight to that pro’s Angi Profile where they can get more information about the pro and make a quote request. Thumbtack is on Stein’s list however Thumbtack did not announce an AI Mode plan via press releases as of Nov. 4.

For home service businesses, the platform they picked to run jobs or find customers now also affects whether they can take booking and quote requests from Google’s AI search. What it takes to qualify differs by platform, down to whether a Google Business Profile is required.

Jobber’s and Housecall Pro’s no-lead-fee terms contrast with Google’s own Local Services Ads, whose help page lists a customer’s booking request as a lead advertisers are charged for in the U.S. and Canada. Angi’s annual report says pros pay it fees for consumer matches, but its AI Mode announcement doesn’t say whether those fees apply to quote requests that start in AI Mode.

A business cannot rely solely on qualifying for a partner platform to show up; though Stein’s post does not describe how Google determines which businesses to display in AI mode. On the other hand, Jobber’s help page states if a customer collects client reviews and uses a booking form instead of just a request form then that can help have their business recommended by Google AI mode more frequently.

Customers of Jobber can verify whether their Jobber addresses are the same as those entered into their Google Business Profile. Housecall Pro customers should find out whether their account qualifies with Google AI mode, and Angi pros can check their Angi profile, because according to Angi, the profile information on Angi is where Google’s AI mode sends homeowners to choose from.

Stein listed ServiceTitan as coming soon. A business on none of the listed platforms has no route to direct bookings through AI Mode.

Google’s help page on checking local availability in AI Mode, doesn’t mention partner links. For the latest updates, keep an eye on that page and each partner’s eligibility rules.

#7319. Meta delays commercial terms update indefinitely

The company’s upcoming commercial terms of service update has prompted regulators to seek more insight into the specific details.

Meta’s planned commercial terms of service update has become a significant topic of concern for the company, and it may now be forced to abandon the update altogether in order to avoid additional scrutiny.

Earlier this month, Meta began informing business users of an upcoming update to its commercial terms of service, which included a change in wording that could have allowed Meta to scrape the website of any business that maintained a Facebook or Instagram presence.

Legal experts raised the alarm, which prompted regulatory groups to pose questions about the change.

Meta has maintained that the purpose of the update is not related to data scraping, and is instead to help with data gathering for the sole purpose of ad targeting. Even so, in response to these queries, Meta delayed the launch of the updated terms, shifting the implementation date from Oct. 20 to Nov. 20.

Then last week, as reported by Reuters, Meta said that it could end up delaying the rollout indefinitely in order to address concerns raised by regulatory groups.

Among those is the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, which, according to The Next Web, has opened an investigation into Meta’s commercial terms for businesses. The European Publishers Council is also assessing next steps amid rising concerns about the gathering of business data to power AI models.

It’s impossible to know the intention of Meta’s planned update, but it does seem plausible that the initial update was not intended to empower broad-scale data-scraping, and that Meta’s inclusion of the term “scraping,” which has a different context in the AI era, has caused this new issue.

But either way, Meta is now working to address concerns ahead of the planned update.

Meta has made a copy of its updated commercial terms available for review, with a note at the top of the screen still indicating that they will go into effect on Nov. 20.

#7314. Businesses Treat Your AI Agent 3 Different Ways via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

An AI agent does things its customer would not, on that customer’s behalf. Three businesses answered that problem three ways in October.

People are starting to send AI agents to do things for them online: Buy the groceries, book the flight, check the bank balance. The agent goes to the business’s website and acts in the customer’s place. Every business now has to decide what to do when one shows up, and in October three big ones answered three different ways.

I think Walmart got it right: It is about to give each agent a separate profile inside the customer’s account. An AI agent will do things the person maybe wouldn’t have, so the two are not the same. But it does those things on the person’s behalf, so they need to be linked. A separate profile lets the business see both: the agent and the customer who sent it.

Walmart says why it built Agent Profiles: “Today, when a customer uses an AI agent, it signs in using a customer’s account. This means that all purchases – whether made by the customer or the agent – appear together, without any differentiation.”

An agent might browse more pages than the customer would, maybe all of them. That’s the most basic difference. Beyond that, it could be literally anything.

So it’s not as simple as letting the agent sign in as the customer. Send a dog to shop for you at a local market, with a set amount of money. The dog only does it to bring the shopping back to you, and the whole thing only makes sense if the sellers know who sent the dog.

Walmart’s spending limit is the set amount of money, and the profile is the sellers knowing who sent it. A block stops the customer from using an agent at all. A shared login hides the agent behind the customer.

DoorDash says outside AI agents have placed “maybe several hundred orders in total”, in CEO Tony Xu’s words on the Q3 call, as TechCrunch reported. In the same quarter DoorDash handled 993 million orders, more than 10 million a day.

The rules for how an agent tells a business who it is are still a draft. The AI customer-service company Sierra and Meta are writing them as the Personal Agent Protocol: 40-plus companies are helping shape it, and its website named no business using it with customers when I checked on 1 November. On October 30, the draft added a recommendation that agents sign their requests with Web Bot Auth, a proposed way for an agent to prove which company runs it. According to the bot-protection company DataDome, as PPC Land reported, Meta’s Muse agent has been signing some of its requests that way since around 12 October, without an announcement.

Do three things before agents arrive in numbers:

If you can’t tell the agent from the customer, you can’t treat it differently.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Ads are being tested in the community platform's own search results with a select group of advertisers, matched partly by relevance to what people search.

Reddit is testing ads in its own search results pages with a select group of eligible advertisers.

The company announced the test in a short newsroom post on Tuesday and said it will evaluate how users respond so it can refine the experience over time. The post doesn’t say how advertisers were chosen or whether others can ask to join.

“These placements leverage existing ad targeting in search results pages on Reddit, which have high purchase and search intent.”

“Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query.”

The post does not mention what else would factor into which ads appear. In the example, a person searching for “espresso station” might see ads for coffee beans, mugs, or espresso machines, and “home office setup” may lead to advertisements for desks, office chairs, or monitors.

Example screens in the post show the mobile version of the Reddit application after searching for “home office setup”. Each screen shows a card labeled “Ad” containing a picture of a product (with a website address) and a “Shop Now” button. One example shows a card sitting under a blurb citing subreddits as its sources. Another example shows a card placed between two posts.

Brooke Osmundson reported that in October 2024, Reddit extended the keyword targeting it uses in its conversation placements to the Feed of the platform.

In its first quarter shareholder letter, Reddit stated that the product placements allow users searching on the site to browse listings and shop right from within those search results. In a phone call with investors after their Q1 earnings were released (April 30), Chief Operating Officer Jennifer Wong stated that Reddit didn’t “even have ads in certain high growing surfaces like search, for example.” On this same call, CEO Steve Huffman reported that “Search WAUqs are up 30% year-over-year.” Search WAUqs is Reddit’s shorthand for weekly active uniques who search.

During a Q2 investor call, Wong referred to search as “a space that we’re eyeing” for advertising and mentioned that Reddit has the infrastructure “already queued up,” according to Roger Montti. Wong also referenced Shopping Listing Ads, a format that groups several retailers’ products in one module, as examples of the type of advertisements she believes could be used on a search page.

Beyond eligibility, Reddit’s post is also silent regarding the other key elements of how the test works, such as markets, ad format types, ad pricing models, and whether it covers more than the app used in its examples.

Reddit is pitching its search pages to advertisers on the strength of what people type there. For now, Reddit’s search ads are limited to the advertisers it selected for the test. You can ask your Reddit rep whether your account is part of the test and how search impressions would show up in reporting.

Advertisers outside the test can watch for search to appear among Reddit’s ad placements. The post gives no end date for the test and no timeline for adding advertisers.

#7306. Reddit pitches its 1,300 gaming-related communities to brands

The company said that in-app conversations “created and shaped by real players” can drive engagement and influence purchasing decisions.

Reddit shared new data on its evolving in-app gaming conversation with a playbook for advertisers that are seeking to get their promotions in front of gamers and gaming-related audiences.

Based on research conducted by TransUnion, Reddit said that gaming marketers are largely failing to capitalize on the opportunities afforded by its highly engaged communities.

As explained by Reddit: “Reddit is home to more than 1,300 gaming-related communities, where conversations are created and shaped by real players. These communities don't just bring gamers together; they influence discovery, engagement, and even purchasing decisions.”

Underlining this, Reddit shared additional notes on gaming engagement, and what that means for marketing approaches.

First, according to comparative analysis of Reddit promotions, Reddit ads drove an average of $8.58 return-on-ad-spend for gaming advertisers.

The analysis also found that Reddit discussions and engagement led to broader halo effect across other channels, boosting overall interest in the advertised products.

As explained by Reddit: “This means Reddit’s modeled contribution included value beyond its own platform, demonstrating how Reddit can complement other media touchpoints and contribute to broader marketing performance. TV accounted for 18% of Reddit’s total synergy, followed by paid search at 17%, online video at 15%, and paid social at 12%.”

In other words, Reddit’s gaming communities are influential, which can expand the value of in-app promotions.

On the basis of the last point, the analysis suggested that gaming brands have significantly underinvested in Reddit ads, with Reddit representing just 5% of paid social investment, on average.

Of course, that’s assuming that these same trends would hold true if more gaming ads were present in the app. But based on the data included in the analysis, there might be more opportunity and potential for gaming marketers there.

The report also said that brands that ran a full-funnel strategy across key campaign objectives saw 19% stronger overall ROAS than the single-tactic average. The report added that video views delivered the strongest ROAS.

There are some interesting data points here, though the parameters of the study make it impossible to establish a true like-for-like comparison in relative ad spend.

But the indications suggest that Reddit ads could deliver value and unique audience reach for gaming marketers.
